**Surah al-Sharh (The Expansion)**
Eight verses, Meccan

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾

It is narrated from Tawus and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that they used to say: this surah and Surah al-Duha are one surah, and they would recite them in a single rak'ah, without separating them with "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." What prompted them to this view is that the Exalted's words ﴿Did We not expand for you﴾ appear to be a continuation of His words ﴿Did He not find you an orphan﴾ [al-Duha: 6]. But this is not so, because the first was revealed while the Messenger (ﷺ) was distressed by the harm of the disbelievers, so it was a state of trial and constriction of the breast. The second implies that at the time of revelation he was of an expanded breast and a content heart, so how can the two come together?

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾

He asked about the negation of expansion in the form of rebuke, which establishes and affirms the expansion, as if it were said: "We expanded your breast for you." Concerning the expansion of the breast there are two views.

The first: it is narrated that Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him, split open his breast, took out his heart, washed it, purified it from sins, then filled it with knowledge and faith and placed it back in his breast.

Know that al-Qadi [the judge, i.e., al-Qadi Abd al-Jabbar] criticized this report on several grounds:

The first: the report says this event occurred when he (peace be upon him) was a child, and that is one of the miracles, so his prophethood cannot be advanced to that time.

The second: the effect of washing lies in removing physical bodies, and sins are not bodies, so washing has no effect on them.

The third: it is not valid that he would fill the heart with knowledge; rather God creates knowledge in it.

As for the answer to the first: the foreshadowing of a miracle before the time of mission (*irhas*, i.e., a prophetic foreshadowing) is permissible according to us, and it is what is called *irhas*, and similar things concerning the Messenger (peace be upon him) are numerous.

As for the second and third: it is not far-fetched that the appearance of that black blood which they washed from the heart of the Messenger (peace be upon him) was a sign of the heart that inclines toward sins and shrinks from acts of obedience. When they removed it from him, that was a sign that its owner is constant in acts of obedience and guarded against misdeeds, and this was like a sign to the angels that its owner is protected from sin. Also, God does what He wills and decrees what He desires.

The second view: the intended meaning of the expansion of the breast is what pertains to knowledge and obedience. They mentioned several aspects concerning it:

The first: when he (peace be upon him) was sent to jinn and humankind, his breast would become constricted by contending with jinn and humankind and by disavowing every worshipper and object of worship other than God. So God gave him from His signs what was sufficient for everything he bore, and made small in his sight everything of hardship he endured. This was achieved by removing from his heart all worries, leaving in it only this one concern. Thus the concern of provision and dependents never occurred to his mind, and he did not care about what might come to him from their harm, until they became in his eyes less than a fly. He did not shrink in fear of their threats, nor did he incline toward what they wanted. In sum, the expansion of the breast is an expression of his knowledge of the worthlessness of this world and the perfection of the Hereafter. A parallel to this is the Exalted's saying: ﴿So whoever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast for Islam, and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted﴾ [al-An'am: 125]. It is also narrated that they said: "O Messenger of Allah, does the breast expand?" He said: "Yes." They said: "And what is the sign of that?" He said: "Withdrawing from deception, turning in repentance to the abode of eternity, and preparing for death before it descends." The truth of this matter is that sincere faith in God and in His promise and threat obliges a person to asceticism in this world, desire for the Hereafter, and readiness for death.

The second: his breast was opened so that it could bear all the great matters without anxiety, impatience, or change. Rather, in both states of hardship and joy he had an expanded breast, occupied with performing what he was charged with. *Al-sharh* means expansion, and its meaning is relief from worries. The Arabs call grief and worry "constriction of the breast," as in His saying: ﴿And We certainly know that your breast is constricted﴾ [al-Hijr: 97]. Here there are several questions.

The first: why did He mention the breast (*sadr*) and not the heart (*qalb*)? The answer: because the locus of whispering is the breast, as He said: ﴿who whispers into the breasts of people﴾ [al-Nas: 5]. The removal of that whispering and its replacement by motives for good is the expansion, so this expansion is rightly restricted to the breast rather than the heart. Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi said: the heart is the locus of intellect and knowledge, and it is what Satan aims at. Satan comes to the breast, which is the fortress of the heart. When he finds a passage, he raids within it and his troops descend into it, and he spreads within it worries, griefs, and greed. The heart then becomes constricted and finds no pleasure in obedience and no sweetness in Islam. But when the enemy is driven off at the outset, he is prevented, security is attained, the constriction disappears, the breast expands, and it becomes easy for him to perform worship.

The second question: why did He say ﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ and not "Did We not expand your breast?" The answer is in two aspects:

The first: it is as if the Exalted says: "A *lam* for a *lam*." You perform all acts of obedience only for My sake, as He said: ﴿I did not create jinn and humankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56], and ﴿and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14]. So I too do everything I do for your sake.

The second: in it there is an indication that the benefits of the mission return to him (peace be upon him). It is as if the Exalted said: "We expanded your breast only for your sake, not for Mine."

The third question: why did He say ﴿Did We not expand﴾ and not "Did I not expand?" The answer: if we take it as the *nun* of majesty, the meaning is that the greatness of the Benefactor indicates the greatness of the favor, which shows that this expansion is a blessing whose true magnitude minds cannot reach. If we take it as the *nun* of plurality, the meaning is as if the Exalted says: "I did not expand it alone; rather I employed My angels in it. You would see the angels around you and before you, until your heart became strong. You delivered the message while your heart was strong, and awe fell upon them, so they did not give you any answer. Had you been constricted of heart, they would have laughed at you. Glory be to Him who made the strength of your heart a cowardice in them, and the expansion of your breast a constriction in them."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ ﴿Which had weighed down your back﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Al-Mubarrad said: This is to be understood in terms of the meaning of "Did We not expand for you" (alam nashrah), not in terms of its wording, because you would not say "alam waḍa'na" (did We not remove). Rather the meaning of "alam nashrah" is "We have expanded," so the second is understood in terms of the meaning of the first, not the apparent wording. For if it were coordinated with its apparent wording, it would have to be said: "wa-naḍa'u 'anka wizraka" (and We remove from you your burden).

The second issue: The meaning of wizr (burden) is the weight of sin. Its explanation has already passed at His saying: ﴿And they bear their burdens﴾ [al-Nahl: 25], and it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your sins, past and future﴾ [al-Fath: 2].

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Which had weighed down your back﴾, the linguists said: The origin of this is that when the back is burdened with a load, a faint sound called naqīḍ is heard from it, namely the sound of saddles, riding gear and ribs, or the camel when the load weighs on it. So it is a metaphor for what weighed on the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of his burdens.

The third issue [as numbered in the text]: Whoever affirms sin for the prophets (peace be upon them) has argued with this verse.

The answer to this comes from two aspects:

The first: Those who permit minor sins for the prophets (peace be upon them) have interpreted this verse in that sense. It should not be said that His saying ﴿which had weighed down your back﴾ indicates that it was great, so how would that fit minor sins? For we say: The description of it as weighing down the back is only given because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) great distress at its occurrence from him, his grief, and his regret over it, even though it is forgiven. As for the description being due to its effect, that by it he lost a great deal of reward, that is permissible for what Allah the Exalted mentioned. This is the explanation of the speech according to the view of the Mu'tazilah, and there is a difficulty in it: that pardoning minor sins is obligatory upon Allah the Exalted according to al-Qadi, while Allah the Exalted mentioned this verse in the context of favour, and it is known that granting favour for performing an obligation is not permissible.

The second aspect: That this be understood as other than sin, and there are several views on it:

One: Qatadah said: The Prophet (ﷺ) had sins that had passed from him in the Jahiliyyah before prophethood, and they had weighed him down, so He forgave them for him.

Two: What is meant is the lightening of the burdens of prophethood, which weigh on the back, of carrying out its command, preserving its requirements and safeguarding its rights. So Allah the Exalted made that easy for him and removed its weight from him by making it easy for him until it became easy for him.

Three: The burden is what he disliked of their altering the sunnah of the Friend (Khalil, Abraham). He could not prevent them until Allah strengthened him and said to him: ﴿Then follow the religion of Abraham﴾ [al-Nahl: 123].

Four: They are the sins of his community, which became like a burden upon him. What should he do regarding them, until He said: ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33]. So He granted him security from punishment in this world, and promised him intercession in the Hereafter.

Five: Its meaning: We protected you from the burden which would have weighed down your back, had that sin occurred. So He called protection "placing down" metaphorically. Among this is what is reported: that he attended a feast where there was a drum and flutes before the mission, in order to listen; so Allah struck his ear, and nothing woke him except the heat of the sun the next day.

Six: The burden is what befell him of awe and terror at the first meeting with Jibril (peace be upon him), when trembling seized him and he almost threw himself from the mountain. Then he grew stronger until he became accustomed to him and reached a state where he almost threw himself from the mountain out of intense longing.

Seven: The burden is what harm and reviling reached him, until it nearly broke his back and trembling seized him. Then Allah the Exalted strengthened him until he was such that they would wound his face, [and he] would say: "O Allah, guide my people."

Eight: If the revelation of the surah was after the death of Abu Talib and Khadijah, then their parting was a great burden upon him. So He removed the burden from him by raising him up to the heavens, until every angel met him and greeted him, and his remembrance was elevated. Therefore He said: ﴿And We raised high your remembrance﴾.

Nine: What is meant by the burden and weight is the bewilderment he had before the mission. For when, with his complete intellect, he contemplated the great blessings of Allah the Exalted upon him, in that He brought him from non-existence into existence and gave him life, reason and kinds of blessings, the blessings of Allah weighed heavily upon him, and his back nearly broke from shame. This is because he, peace be upon him, saw that Allah's blessings upon him would never end, and he did not know how he should obey his Lord. When prophethood and obligation came to him and he knew how he ought to obey his Lord, then his shame lessened and those states became easy for him. For the base person does not feel shame at increasing blessings without repaying them with service, whereas the generous-spirited person, when favours upon him multiply while he repays them with no kind of service, finds that extremely heavy, to the point that shame nearly kills him. When the Benefactor assigns him some kind of service, that becomes easy for him and his heart is at ease.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ ﴿Which had weighed down your back﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Al-Mubarrad said: This is to be understood in terms of the meaning of "Did We not expand for you" (alam nashrah), not in terms of its wording, because you would not say "alam waḍa'na" (did We not remove). Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We raised high your mention﴾.

Know that this is general to everything they have mentioned concerning prophethood: his fame in the earth and the heavens; his name being written upon the Throne; his name being mentioned with Him in the testimony of faith and in the tashahhud (the formula recited in prayer); that He, exalted is He, mentioned him in the earlier scriptures; the spread of his mention across the horizons; that prophethood was sealed with him; that he is mentioned in the sermons (khutab), in the adhan (call to prayer), and at the openings of letters; and at the conclusion. He also made his mention in the Qur'an joined with His own mention: ﴿But Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [At-Tawbah: 62]; ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ [An-Nisa': 13]; ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 92]. And He calls him by the title of Messenger and Prophet, whereas He calls others by their names: "O Musa," "O 'Isa." Also, He placed him in hearts such that they find his mention sweet. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Most Merciful will appoint for them affection﴾ [Maryam: 6]. It is as if He, exalted is He, is saying: "I will fill the world with your followers, all of whom will praise you, send blessings upon you, and preserve your sunnah. Indeed, there is no obligatory act of the prayer except that with it is a sunnah: they comply in the obligation with My command and in the sunnah with your command. I have made your obedience My obedience and your pledge My pledge: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa': 80]; ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you are actually pledging allegiance to Allah﴾ [Al-Fath: 10]." Rulers do not disdain your followers. Rather, it would be an audacity of the most ignorant kings to appoint a caliph who is not from your tribe. So the reciters preserve the wording of your decree, the exegetes explain the meanings of your Criterion (Furqan), and the preachers convey your admonition. Indeed, scholars and rulers come to serve you, greet you from behind the door, wipe their faces with the dust of your garden (rawdah), and hope for your intercession. Thus your nobility endures until the Day of Resurrection.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 94, verses 5–6:

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So indeed with hardship comes ease.﴾ ﴿Indeed, with hardship comes ease.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: the connection of this verse with what precedes it. The polytheists used to reproach the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for his poverty, saying: "If your aim in what you claim is to seek wealth, we will gather wealth for you until you become like the wealthiest of the people of Makkah." This distressed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to the extent that it occurred to him that they had only turned away from Islam because he was poor and despised among them. So God, exalted is He, enumerated His favours upon him in this surah and said: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾, meaning what you were burdened with from the affairs of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance). Then He promised him worldly wealth, in order to remove from his heart the distress that had arisen in it because they reproached him for his poverty. The evidence for this is the entry of the particle fa' (فَ) into His words: ﴿So indeed with hardship comes ease﴾, as if He, exalted is He, had said: Do not let what they say grieve you, nor your present scarcity, for there will come to you in this world complete ease.

The second issue: Ibn 'Abbas said: God, exalted is He, says: "I created one hardship between two eases, so one hardship will never overcome two eases." Muqatil narrated from the Prophet, upon whom be prayers and peace, that he said: "''One hardship will never overcome two eases''," and he recited this verse. In explaining this meaning there are two aspects:

The first: al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the word "hardship" (al-'usr) is mentioned with the definite article (alif and lam, الألف واللام), and there is no previously known referent, so it is taken to refer to the reality itself, and therefore the word "hardship" in both instances refers to one and the same thing. As for "ease" (al-yusr), it is mentioned in an indefinite form (tankir, التنكير, indefiniteness), so the two are different. Al-Jurjani rejected this view and said: if a man says, "Indeed, with the horseman is a sword, indeed, with the horseman is a sword," it would necessarily imply that there is one horseman with two swords, and it is known that this does not follow from the usage of the Arabic language.

The second aspect: the second clause is a repetition of the first, just as God repeated His words: ﴿Woe that Day to the deniers﴾ [al-Mursalat: 15]. The purpose is to fix its meaning in souls and to establish it in hearts, just as a single word is repeated in your saying: "Zayd came to me, Zayd, Zayd." By "the two eases" is meant: the ease of this world, which is what became easy of conquering lands, and the ease of the Hereafter, which is the reward of Paradise, in accordance with His words: ﴿Say: Do you await for us anything but one of the two best outcomes?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 52], and these two are the good of victory and the good of reward. Thus the meaning of His words, "''One hardship will never overcome two eases''," is this. That is because the lifespan of this world, in comparison with the ease of this world and the ease of the Hereafter, is like something small and submerged.

Here there are two questions.

The first: what is the significance of the indefiniteness in "ease"? Its answer: it is for magnification (al-tafkhim, التفخيم), as if it were said: "Indeed, with ease, is an ease, indeed, with hardship, is a great ease, and what an ease!"

The second question: ease cannot coexist with hardship, since they are opposites and therefore cannot come together. The answer: since the occurrence of ease after hardship is only a short time later, it is considered certain, and so it is treated as if it were concurrent with it.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when you are free, then strive hard﴾. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah enumerated His past blessings upon him and promised him future blessings, He naturally moved him to gratitude and to diligence in worship, so He said: ﴿So when you are free, then strive hard﴾, i.e., exert yourself and toil. It is said: nasaba (نَصَبَ) yanṣibu. Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: when you finish the obligatory prayer, ﴿then strive hard and turn to your Lord﴾ [al-Sharh: 7] in supplication, and desire Him in your request, and He will give to you. Al-Sha'bi said: when you finish the tashahhud, supplicate for your worldly life and your Hereafter. Mujahid said: when you finish the affairs of your worldly life, then strive hard and pray. ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) said: when you finish the obligatory duties, then strive hard in the night prayer. Al-Hasan said: when you finish the military campaign, then exert yourself in worship. ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah said: when you are healthy, then strive hard, meaning: make your free time a toil in worship. This is supported by what is reported that Shurayh passed by two men wrestling, and said: "The one who is free is not commanded to do this; rather Allah only said: ﴿So when you are free, then strive hard﴾." In sum, the meaning is that one should link some acts of worship with others, not leaving any part of his time free of them, and when he finishes one act of worship, he follows it with another.
* * *
As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And to your Lord turn eagerly﴾, there are two interpretations:
The first: make your desire directed to Him exclusively, and ask only for His bounty, relying upon Him.

The second: desire from your Lord everything you seek, in religion, in worldly life, and in victory over enemies. It is also read as fa-raghghib (فَرَغِّبْ), i.e., make people desire what is with Him. And Allah, glory be to Him, knows best, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when you are free, then strive hard﴾. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah enumerated His past blessings upon him and promised him future blessings, He naturally moved him to gratitude and to diligence in worship, so He said: ﴿So when you are free, then strive hard﴾, i.e., exert yourself and toil. It is said: nasaba (نَصَبَ) yanṣibu. Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: when you finish the obligatory prayer, ﴿then strive hard and turn to your Lord﴾ [al-Sharh: 7] in supplication, and desire Him in your request, and He will give to you. Al-Sha'bi said: when you finish the tashahhud, supplicate for your worldly life and your Hereafter. Mujahid said: when you finish the affairs of your worldly life, then strive hard and pray. ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) said: when you finish the obligatory duties, then strive hard in the night prayer. Al-Hasan said: when you finish the military campaign, then exert yourself in worship. ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah said: when you are healthy, then strive hard, meaning: make your free time a toil in worship. This is supported by what is reported that Shurayh passed by two men wrestling, and said: "The one who is free is not commanded to do this; rather Allah only said: ﴿So when you are free, then strive hard﴾." In sum, the meaning is that one should link some acts of worship with others, not leaving any part of his time free of them, and when he finishes one act of worship, he follows it with another.
* * *
As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And to your Lord turn eagerly﴾, there are two interpretations:
The first: make your desire directed to Him exclusively, and ask only for His bounty, relying upon Him.

The second: desire from your Lord everything you seek, in religion, in worldly life, and in victory over enemies. It is also read as fa-raghghib (فَرَغِّبْ), i.e., make people desire what is with Him. And Allah, glory be to Him, knows best, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.
